sn42.6:1.1: Pāvārika means “blanket-weaver”. Places were often named for their primary economic activity. Probably there was a community of blanket weavers and the park was owned by their leading merchant. See too note at [mn56:2.1]().
sn42.6:1.2: Asibandhaka’s son appears in each discourse up to [sn42.9](). His father’s name “Swordstrap”, following on the previous discourses, suggests a military connection (cf. _asibaddha_, “sword-strapped”, Śāṅkhāyana Śrautasūtra 14.22.20); but the texts do not confirm this.
sn42.6:2.1: The “western brahmins” (_brāhmaṇā pacchā bhūmakā_) hail from lands such as Kuru and Pañcālā or further west to Gandhārā. They are depicted as adherents of ritualism, in contrast with the brahmins of the lands of the Buddha, especially Kosala, who were more aligned with the contemplative and philosophical teachings of the Upaniṣads. This tension is felt in the Upaniṣads themselves, as Yājñavalkya  is accused of flouting the teachings of the Vedic scholars of Kuru and Pañcālā (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.19). | A “pitcher” (_kāmaṇḍalu_) of water was carried at all times to ensure personal hygiene (Manu 4.36). | I have not been able to identify the practice of “garlanding with aquatic flowers” (_sevālamālikā_). The term appears a couple of times in the Harivaṁsa (_śaivālamala_), but of trees (55.53) or a disheveled woman (83.38), where it seems to mean “moss”. It seems unlikely that brahmins would smear moss on themselves. The commentary says, “Bright and early, having taken _sevāla_ or lotus, etc. from the water, they make a decorative garland for the sake of identifying those who believe in purification by water.” The emphasis on collecting the flowers at dawn hints at a connection with the Sun, who rises from the ocean each day (cf. Sāhityakaumudī 10.258). The malicious _yakkha_ of [dn23:23.13]() intimates the presence of water with his garland of yellow lotus (_kumudamāli_); he appears on a trade journey, probably to the west. The plant was probably a kind of *Vallisneria*, which grows profusely underwater, sending its small white flowers to the surface.
sn42.6:2.2: I take the particle _nāma_ here as indicating wonder. | Resolve _saññāpenti_ as _saṁ yāpenti_, “they send them well”.
sn42.6:4.3: For “supplication” (_āyācana_) see too [an5.43:3.1]() and [dn13:16.2](). | For _anuparisakkeyya_ (“circumambulate”), see Sanskrit _ṣvaṣk_, “go, move”.
sn42.6:4.6: The Buddha argues that personal action rather than religious ritual determines rebirth.
sn42.6:7.1: At Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.6.2–3, Uddālaka compares the ghee that arises as curd is churned to the mind.
